items.label: Topic Intro
items.text: Today's topic is Why a Notification Can Steal Focus Before You Check Your Phone.

items.label: Preview
items.text: This episode asks a simple question: Can a phone affect your attention before you check it? The question matters whenever you are trying to work or study. We will look at research on this problem and ask what not checking really means. By the end, you will have a clearer way to think about phones and focus.

items.label: Comment 1
items.text: Listen for the different phone situations in the two studies while the students did their tasks.

items.label: Full Story Part 1
items.text:
Imagine you are working. Your phone makes a sound. You do not pick it up or even look at the screen. Still, the moment feels different. Research suggests that distraction may begin before you check.

Two peer-reviewed studies help explain why. In a 2022 study, 73 university students completed a visual task while either a notification sound or an unrelated comparison sound played. They did not look at or touch a phone. Even so, the sound affected how they handled the task.

A 2023 study examined a quieter situation. Forty-two university students took a concentration test with a powered-off smartphone on the desk or in another room. No notifications were received. This study also found a difference between the two settings.

items.label: Comment 2
items.text: The studies suggest that a phone can affect attention even when you do not check it. How does this pull appear in everyday life, especially for teenagers?

items.label: Full Story Part 2
items.text:
At first, this seems like a story about willpower. But the studies point to two separate pressures. One comes from the sound. The other comes from the device being part of the workspace. Together, they suggest that “not checking” is not the same as “not being affected.” The studies used specific tasks and university students, so they do not show that every phone affects every person in every situation.

Outside the lab, this pull is also part of daily life for many US teens. In a 2018 survey of teens aged 13 to 17, 72% said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications soon after waking. When their phone was not with them, 56% reported feeling anxious, lonely, upset, or some combination of these. A majority also said they felt a need to reply quickly to texts, social-media messages, or other notifications.

items.label: Comment 3
items.text: This story is not only about choosing to check a phone. The studies and the survey suggest that a phone can affect people even when they do not check it. Now, let’s look more closely at what may be happening in these situations.

items.label: Point One (heading)
items.text: The hidden cost comes before the check

items.label: Point One
items.text: The key shift is from behavior to effort. A person can keep their hands off the phone and still pay a price on the very trial when the sound appears. Responses were slower, while a brain-wave signal associated with cognitive control became larger. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that staying on task required extra mental effort after the notification sound.

items.label: Point Two (heading)
items.text: A quiet phone can still take up space

items.label: Point Two
items.text: The second experiment did not compare a ringing phone with a silent phone. It compared a powered-off phone on the desk with that phone in another room. Attention scores were about 100 versus 109, and processing-speed scores were about 98 versus 109. For work or study, moving the device may address something that muting does not.

items.label: Comment 4
items.text: The two points suggest that a phone’s effect may not be easy to see. It can require extra effort, and its location may matter even when it is not being used. Now, let’s bring the main message together.

items.label: In One Line
items.text: A notification may interrupt focus through its sound, while a silent phone may still compete through its presence. Protecting attention may involve not only resisting the urge to check, but also reducing the phone’s chance to enter the task.

items.label: Topic Intro
items.text: Today's topic is The Notification You Hear Without Looking.

items.label: Japanese Title
items.text: 通知を無視するのが、なぜこんなに難しいのか

items.label: Preview
items.text: スマホを使っていない時間にも、集中は影響を受けるのでしょうか。今回のニュースでは、二つの研究を通して、見た目には分かりにくい注意の変化と、作業への関わりを見ていきます。

items.label: Comment 1
items.text: 学生がスマホを見たり触ったりしなくても、通知音のあとに作業へどんな変化が出たのかに注目してください。

items.label: Full Story Part 1
items.text:
A phone does not need to light up in your hand to change a task. A sound may be enough. In another study, even a silent phone on a desk was linked to lower attention.

A 2022 study tested 73 college students. They worked through a letter task. In some trials, they heard a notification sound. In others, they heard a neutral sound. They did not look at or touch a phone.

The result was clear: responses were slower during trials with notification sounds. Brain recordings also showed a larger signal after those sounds. This happened even though the students kept working and did not check a screen.

items.label: Comment 2
items.text: 通知音だけでも、画面を見なくても、作業中の反応は遅くなりました。では、音も通知もないスマホが近くにあるだけでも、作業の結果は変わるのでしょうか。

items.label: Full Story Part 2
items.text:
A second study, published in 2023, tested 42 university students. Their phones were powered off, and no notifications arrived. The researchers compared a phone on the desk with a phone in another room.

Performance was lower when the phone stayed on the desk. The attention score averaged 99.71 on the desk, compared with 108.95 when the phone was away. Processing speed was 98.48 on the desk and 108.57 in another room.

Together, these studies show two different moments. A notification can affect a person during a task. A phone can also be linked to lower performance without making a sound.

items.label: Comment 3
items.text: このニュースは、スマートフォンが、画面を見たり音を聞いたりする場面だけでなく、作業中の注意や成績とも関係することを示しています。これからは、まず見えにくい負担に目を向け、そのあとで、音を消すことと、そこにないことの違いを見ていきます。

items.label: Point One (heading)
items.text: The cost you cannot see

items.label: Point One
items.text: Distraction is not always a visible choice. Someone can keep working and still spend more effort staying with the task. The researchers read the slower responses and larger brain signal as a sign of that extra control. So a person who never checks the screen may still pay an attention cost.

items.label: Point Two (heading)
items.text: Muting is not the same as absence

items.label: Point Two
items.text: A silent phone is not the same as no phone. The second study suggests that silencing alerts and moving the device may address different problems, although it did not test either action as a solution. The social side matters too: 72% of U.S. teens often or sometimes checked messages or notifications soon after waking. And 56% reported at least one of anxiety, loneliness, or upset when their phone was not nearby.

items.label: Comment 4
items.text: ここまで、スマートフォンを見ていなくても、仕事中の注意に負担がかかる場合があることを見てきました。また、通知を消すことと、端末を近くに置かないことは同じではありません。ここからは、この二つを踏まえたニュース全体の要点を英語で聞いてみましょう。

items.label: In One Line
items.text: These studies suggest a quiet lesson: attention can be pulled by a sound, or shared with a phone that never rings.
